cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Choose What Matters More
cards.instruction: Make someone choose between emotional safety and the outcome they claim to want.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. Before we renew this lease, do you want my honest answer about living together or a peaceful dinner?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Your honest answer. Just don't say anything that makes me panic.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. I can't promise both. Shall I answer, or shall we order?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Answer. But start by saying we're fine.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: That's the answer you're choosing for me. Do you still want mine?

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 controls timing and A3 refuses both guarantees, but A5 ordinary do-you-still-want question does not consistently use superior approval beyond the stock phrases.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 wants honesty without panic prompts A3 answer/order choice; B4 reassuring preface demand prompts A5 naming the preselected answer.

relationship.evidence: B2 fear of distress and B4 attempt to secure reassurance are plausible and directly expose the trade-off.

heightening.evidence: B4 scripted fine turns A5 from general risk warning to the specific problem of choosing A answer in advance.

specificity.evidence: A1 lease renewal and dinner establish decision and setting; the true answer may remain unknown because choosing to hear it is the current task.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 answer you choose for me is earned, while the stock rank preface is redundant.
